newsitem.title: GIBRALTAR: Hassan, ex-Gibraltar chief minister, dead at 81.
newsitem.headline: Hassan, ex-Gibraltar chief minister, dead at 81.

text.p: Sir Joshua Hassan, a former Gibraltar chief minister who led fierce resistance to Spain's claim of sovereignty over the tiny British colony, died on Tuesday. He was 81 years old.
Hassan died of natural causes after lapsing in a coma one day after being admitted to Gibraltar's St. Bernard's Hospital, a family spokesman said.
Gibraltar's first mayor and first chief minister, Hassan dominated the colony's political scene for more than four decades and was reputed to have known almost all of its residents by name.

He based his political career on the premise that the citizens of Gibraltar -- a rocky outcrop ceded to Britain in 1713 under the Treaty of Utrecht -- alone had the right to decide their fate and the vast majority wanted to remain British.

Twice in the 1960s, he led petitioners from "The Rock" to testify in New York before the United Nations Committee on Decolonisation, and in 1967 he put his principle to the test with a referendum on the colony's future.
The public's verdict was overwhelming -- 12,138 votes in favor of remaining with Britain and only 44 votes against.

His persistence was rewarded in 1969 when Britain drew up a new constitution that pledged it would "never enter into arrangements under which the people of Gibraltar would pass under the sovereignty of another state against their freely and democratically expressed wishes."
In retaliation, Spanish dictator Francisco Franco gradually sealed off access to Gibraltar by land and sea, culminating in full closure of the border in June 1969.

After five years as chief minister, Hassan lost the post in the general election that year when his party failed by one seat to win a majority. But he was voted back into power in 1972 and remained there for the next 15 years.

The frontier was not reopened until 1985, more than nine years after Franco's death when democratic Spain was seeking to join the European Community. But tensions have lingered, with Spain regularly reasserting its claim.
Born in Gibraltar in 1915, Hassan studied law at the Middle Temple in London and was called to the bar in 1939.
His political career began during World War Two when he served as a gunner in the Gibraltar Defence Force and most of the local poulation had been evacuated.

As suspicions grew that Britain was having second thoughts about returning the colony's civilian population after the war, Hassan became a founding member of the Association for the Advancement of Civil Rights in 1942.
He headed the city and legislative councils for all but three of the years from 1945 to 1969, when they were merged into the present House of Assembly.
Hassan retired from politics in 1987, citing personal reasons.
But he remained an influential and often outspoken figure. Last December, he was honoured with an award known as the "Freedom of the City of Gibraltar."
